title: Diplomatic Simulator
summary: An interactive simulation of multi-party diplomatic negotiation in which human or AI participants role-play state actors through a geopolitical crisis, producing a transcript, tactic analysis and convener report.

contribution.roleNote: Yorke authored 27 of 98 human commits; Carolina Moron authored the rest.

narrative.problem: Multi-party crises such as the Arctic, the Fergana Valley, Cyprus, the South China Sea, the Korean peninsula and Kashmir involve many delegations with confidential positions, and it is hard to rehearse or study how such negotiations unfold, which tactics appear and what survives as agreement.
narrative.decision: Each delegation is played by an AI agent (Claude Opus 4.8 in the baseline) driven by its own confidential privileged instructions, with information isolated between seats, and every run produces a full transcript, tactic analysis and convener report.
narrative.tradeoff: Results describe how one model behaves playing every side, not how negotiations behave; and because authorised concessions and demands never overlap, the audit found no scenario is settleable by construction, so zero settlements measures the scenario pack.
narrative.limitation: A working prototype whose independent peer review recommends major revisions. The mixed-model check is one Korea run per condition with model and role confounded, Monte Carlo uses about 20 trials per scenario, and the paper says results should not yet be read as findings about negotiation.
narrative.caveat: All negotiation content is generated by AI agents (Claude Opus 4.8) role-playing each delegation and is notional and for educational use only; search indexing is disabled so invented statements are not mistaken for reporting.
